title: Nuclear fission and fusion (physics only)

final_note: You worked through Nuclear fission and fusion (physics only) — 8 specification statements.

concepts.def: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, for example a uranium or a plutonium nucleus. It is a change to the nucleus itself, not a rearrangement of atoms or electrons.
A nucleus holding a very large number of protons and neutrons that is not stable, such as uranium or plutonium. Only nuclei of this kind undergo fission; small stable nuclei do not.
Fission that happens on its own, without the nucleus being struck by anything. It is rare, which is why fission fuel does not simply split apart by itself while it is in storage.
Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Neutrons are uncharged, so they are not repelled as they approach the nucleus.
What a fission event produces: two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, together with two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
Energy is released by the fission reaction. It appears as the kinetic energy of the products and as the gamma radiation emitted.

concepts.term: Kinetic energy of the fission products
concepts.def: All of the fission products have kinetic energy: the two smaller nuclei and the two or three neutrons all move away from the split at speed.
The neutrons released by one fission may go on to be absorbed by other unstable nuclei, causing those nuclei to undergo fission and release further neutrons in turn.
The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so that the rate of fission and the energy output stay steady.
A chain reaction in which the number of fissions grows very rapidly. The explosion caused by a nuclear weapon is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

concepts.term: Mass converted into the energy of radiation
concepts.def: In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus formed has less mass than the two light nuclei had between them.

options: The joining of two light nuclei into a single heavier nucleus.
The breaking of a nucleus into its separate protons and neutrons.
The splitting of a small, stable nucleus such as a carbon nucleus.
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus such as a uranium nucleus.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium.

mcqs.q: A power station uses uranium as its fuel. Why can a uranium nucleus undergo fission when a carbon nucleus cannot?
options: A carbon nucleus is stable and is far too small to be split.
A uranium nucleus is large and unstable, so it can split.
A uranium atom holds more electrons than a carbon atom.
A carbon nucleus can only join to others, never split.
mcqs.explain: Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, eg uranium or plutonium; a small stable nucleus such as carbon does not undergo fission.

mcqs.q: Spontaneous fission is rare. What must usually happen before a large unstable nucleus undergoes fission?
options: The unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
The unstable nucleus must be heated to a high temperature.
The unstable nucleus must first absorb a proton.
The unstable nucleus must first absorb a gamma ray.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that usually, for fission to occur, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.

mcqs.q: A uranium nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission. Apart from gamma rays, what does the fission produce?
options: Two smaller nuclei of about the same size, and a single extra neutron.
One large nucleus and one very small nucleus, plus a few free neutrons.
Two smaller nuclei of roughly equal size, plus two or three neutrons.
A shower of individual protons and neutrons from the nucleus that split.
mcqs.explain: The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.

mcqs.q: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. Which statement about the two nuclei it produces is correct?
options: They are stable, so no further radiation is ever emitted by them.
They are roughly equal in size, and both are smaller than the uranium nucleus.
One is much larger than the other, and the smaller is a proton.
They are identical to each other, right down to the mass number.
mcqs.explain: The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size.

mcqs.q: In a fission event, which of the products are given kinetic energy?
options: Only the two smaller nuclei that are formed by the split.
None of them, since the energy is carried off by the gamma rays.
Only the neutrons, which then go on to cause more fission.
All of them, including each of the neutrons that are emitted.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that all of the fission products have kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Why can a single fission event lead to a chain reaction?
options: The gamma rays given out are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
The energy released heats the fuel up until the nuclei around it break apart.
The neutrons released are absorbed by other nuclei, making those split too.
The two nuclei that are formed split again into even smaller ones.
mcqs.explain: The neutrons emitted may go on to start a chain reaction: each absorbed neutron can cause a further fission.

mcqs.q: How does the chain reaction inside a nuclear reactor differ from the one in a nuclear weapon?
options: In the reactor it is controlled; in the weapon it is not.
The reactor releases energy slowly because it uses a different fuel.
The reactor splits nuclei, while the weapon works by joining them.
The reactor uses a chain reaction, but the weapon does not use one.
mcqs.explain: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, whereas the weapon's explosion is caused by an uncontrolled chain reaction.

mcqs.q: The chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled. What does controlling it achieve?
options: It keeps the rate of fission steady, so the energy is released steadily.
It stops the chain reaction, so that no further fission takes place.
It makes the reaction spread faster, so more energy is given out.
It removes the gamma rays produced, so no radiation escapes.
mcqs.explain: The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released, so the core delivers energy steadily instead of all at once.

mcqs.q: A student is drawing a chain reaction diagram. One neutron causes a fission that releases three neutrons, and each of those is absorbed by another uranium nucleus. What should the diagram show next?
options: One further fission, with the two spare neutrons simply stopping there.
Three further fissions, each of them releasing three more neutrons.
Three further fissions, each of them releasing one new neutron.
Three bursts of gamma radiation spreading out from the nuclei.
mcqs.explain: Each absorbed neutron causes a fission that emits two or three neutrons of its own, so the diagram branches: one, then three, then nine.

options: Two heavy nuclei join together to form one lighter nucleus.
A large unstable nucleus splits into two fragments.
Two light nuclei join to form a single heavier nucleus.
Two atoms bond together to make a molecule with one nucleus.
mcqs.explain: Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

mcqs.q: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. What may happen to some of their mass?
options: It is thrown out of the new nucleus as extra neutrons.
It stays the same, since mass is always conserved.
It is used up in splitting the new nucleus apart.
It is converted into the energy of radiation.
mcqs.explain: In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
